title: How we separate today's wedding experience from future plans

content.job: Standalone written account of the whole exchange, including Whitney's ideal-couple prompt, the owner's clarification and Whitney's answer. Keep the interpretation limited to the distinction established in this conversation.
content.body:
I told her I meant something closer to what actually happens, like what a current couple is experiencing.

I had used an ideal-couple prompt, so her clarification was reasonable. The invitation could have led to an envisioned wedding day or an account of current events. She asked which one I meant.

For that part of our conversation, I was requesting the present-day experience.

**A venue's direction and a current couple's day can be understood without being merged into one story.**

If you're developing the next chapter of your venue, you may have a detailed picture of the weddings you want to host in the future. That picture can be meaningful alongside the experience of couples there now.

One account describes where you're taking the business. The other describes what a couple currently experiences. Both can have a place in the discussion, while remaining different accounts.

In this exchange, the owner named that distinction and I clarified the scope of the walkthrough. There was no need to make her vision part of the present-day description for it to matter in the conversation.
content.ending:
Whoever helps with your marketing should be curious about where your venue is going, and precise about which wedding day they're hoping to hear about when they ask.

Talk soon,
Whitney

content.title: Which wedding day she asked about
content.script:
A venue owner asked me which wedding day I wanted her to describe.

I had asked her to help me picture her ideal couple's wedding day. And she asked whether that would be visualizing what she'd love to see, or what actually happens.

That's a fair question, right? An ideal-couple prompt could take that conversation in either direction.

I clarified that I meant what a current couple was experiencing. So, for that walkthrough, I was asking her to describe the day as it happens.

I think there's room for that distinction when you're growing a venue. You can have a clear picture of what you want future weddings to look like and still have an experience happening now that deserves its own description.

Both can be part of the discussion. They just give us different accounts of the venue.

In this exchange, the owner asked which one I wanted, and I specified the current experience. Her plans didn't need to become part of that description for them to have a place in the conversation.

caption.body:
There's the day your couples have now: when they arrive, how they use the spaces, how the afternoon flows. And there's the day you're building toward, the one you picture when you think about where the venue is going.

Both are real to you. Both matter when you talk about your marketing. They just answer different questions.

In a recent strategy conversation, I invited a venue owner to walk me through her ideal couple's wedding day. Before she went on, she asked which version I meant: the one she envisioned, or what currently happens.

She was the one who drew that line. I clarified that I wanted a current couple's experience for that walkthrough. Nothing about that answer set her plans aside. It simply made clear which account we were talking about in that moment.

When you're developing what comes next for a venue, you deserve a team that makes room for where you're headed and still asks what your couples are experiencing right now.

content.title: Her plans belong in the conversation
content.script:
I think a venue owner's vision for the future deserves a real place in a strategy conversation. I just don't think it should get blended into the description of the weddings she's hosting today.

Here's what I mean. If you're growing a venue, you're probably holding two pictures at once. There's what couples experience at your venue right now, and there's what you're building toward. Both of those matter when we're talking about your marketing. They're just different accounts.

I saw this come up on a call recently. I asked a venue owner to walk me through her ideal couple's wedding day, and she asked whether I wanted the day she envisioned or the day as it currently happens. She made that distinction herself. I told her I meant what a current couple experiences.

That didn't take anything away from her plans. It just meant we both knew which day we were talking about.

So if you're working on your venue's next chapter, I think the right people around you will want to hear about both, and they'll be clear with you about which one they're asking for.

caption.body:
Maybe you're getting clearer on the weddings you want to be known for, or picturing how the venue will feel a few years from now. That thinking matters, and it shapes how you talk about your business.

At the same time, couples are booking and getting married there right now, and their day has its own shape.

I asked a venue owner recently to walk me through her ideal couple's wedding day. She asked me whether I wanted the day she pictured or the day couples currently have. I told her I meant a current couple's experience. She was the one who named the difference.

I don't see that as choosing one over the other. Her vision still had a place in our conversation. It just wasn't the same account as a couple's day at her venue today.

When you're building something bigger, you should be able to share both with the people behind your marketing and trust that they know which one they're hearing.

That's what I want for every owner building something bigger: room to talk about where you're going, and a team that's clear about which wedding day it's asking about.

changes.after:
If you're investing in a venue's growth, you probably know both versions well. There's the day couples have with you now. And there's the day you picture as the venue keeps evolving.

It's easy for those to run together when someone asks you to describe your weddings. You're proud of what's happening now, and you're excited about what's coming.

On a recent strategy call, I invited a venue owner to walk me through her ideal couple's day. She asked whether I meant the experience she hoped for or the one happening now. I specified a current couple's experience.

She raised that distinction on her own. My answer gave the walkthrough a clear subject, with her vision kept as its own story.

That's what I want for every owner building something bigger: room to talk about where you're going, and a team that's clear about which wedding day it's asking about.
changes.before:
When you're putting thought into how your venue will evolve, that vision is part of what you bring to a conversation about advertising. It can sit alongside your knowledge of the weddings you host, rather than taking the place of that knowledge.

One owner made the distinction herself during a strategy discussion. After I invited her to describe an ideal couple's day, she asked whether I meant the experience she hoped for or the events currently taking place. I specified the experience of a current couple.

That gave this particular walkthrough a defined subject. We were discussing the present-day wedding, while the owner's envisioned experience remained a separate account.

I see room for both when talking about a growing venue. Hearing the direction an owner wants to take doesn't require treating that direction as a description of current events. Here, her clarification and my response established which account we were discussing.
